question: Why do nurses need to ask about the type of creature and time of the incident during an assessment?

options.A: It helps determine the correct treatment and predicts potential complications
options.B: It eliminates the need to monitor vital signs over time
options.C: It prevents the patient from panicking about the injury
options.D: It satisfies hospital billing and administrative record requirements

explanation: Knowing what bit or stung the patient (and when!) helps you anticipate symptoms, choose the right antivenom if needed, and watch for trouble early.

question: How does a dangerously fast heart rate hurt the heart's own blood supply?

options.A: It shortens the resting phase when the heart fills with blood.
options.B: It blocks the electrical signals from the SA node.
options.C: It increases the pressure inside the coronary sinus.
options.D: It causes the aortic valve to close too early.

explanation: Exactly! When the heart beats too fast, diastole gets too short, meaning the heart muscle misses out on its proper resting and feeding time.

question: Which dietary recommendation is most important for a patient recovering from a severe bone infection?

options.A: Low calorie intake to prevent any weight gain during bed rest
options.B: Strictly liquid diet to rest the digestive system after surgery
options.C: High sodium diet to maintain normal blood pressure levels
options.D: High protein and vitamin C intake to promote tissue and bone healing

explanation: Healing bone requires adequate nutrition, particularly proteins and vitamins, to rebuild damaged cellular matrix and fight infection. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h9)

question: When is a return-to-work medical examination performed?

options.A: Before a new worker signs their initial employment contract
options.B: Every month as a routine check for all factory staff members
options.C: After an employee recovers from an illness or injury and prepares to resume duties
options.D: Immediately after a major chemical spill occurs on site

explanation: Spot on! This check ensures the worker is fully ready to return or tells us if they need lighter duties to avoid getting hurt again.

question: What is the main job of the tiny bones (ossicles) inside your middle ear?

options.A: To amplify and transmit sound vibrations to the cochlea
options.B: To filter and warm incoming air before it reaches the lungs
options.C: To produce endolymph and maintain fluid pressure in the inner ear
options.D: To equalize air pressure between the ear canal and the throat

explanation: The malleus, incus, and stapes work together like a tiny lever system to boost the strength of sound waves as they travel from the air into the fluid-filled inner ear. Brilliant work!

question: What should an auxiliary nurse do if asked to perform a procedure they have never been taught?

options.A: Refuse the task and inform the nurse of their lack of training
options.B: Ignore the instruction and leave the ward immediately
options.C: Attempt the procedure quietly to avoid upsetting senior staff
options.D: Ask another patient to guide them through the steps

explanation: It takes courage, but speaking up keeps patients safe. Never attempt unfamiliar clinical procedures without proper training.

question: What is the safest way to bend down and pick up a heavy item off the floor?

options.A: Bend at your knees and hips while keeping your back straight
options.B: Twist your upper body sideways as you reach down
options.C: Arch your back backward before lifting upward
options.D: Bend forward only at your waist with stiff knees

explanation: Always let your strong leg muscles do the heavy lifting instead of your back! Keeping your back straight protects your spine.

question: At what age does a baby get their first dose of the measles vaccine?

options.A: At 9 months of age
options.B: At birth
options.C: At 6 weeks of age
options.D: At 14 weeks of age

explanation: Exactly! We wait until 9 months because antibodies passed down from the mother can block the measles vaccine if given too early.

question: Why is an oxytocic medicine a must-have in your home delivery bag?

options.A: To actively manage the third stage of labor and prevent bleeding
options.B: To help dilate the cervix more quickly in early labor
options.C: To relieve severe labor pain during the second stage
options.D: To stimulate milk production before the baby is born

explanation: You got it! Oxytocin makes the uterus clamp down strongly after delivery, which is our absolute best defense against heavy postpartum bleeding.

question: Why does the pancreas release bicarbonate ions into the small intestine?

options.A: To stimulate the gallbladder to release stored bile
options.B: To neutralize acidic chyme coming from the stomach
options.C: To break down complex proteins into amino acids
options.D: To lower blood sugar levels after a heavy meal

explanation: Food coming from the stomach is super acidic. The pancreas sends out bicarbonate (think of it like natural baking soda) to calm down that acid so it doesn't burn your intestines!

question: Why must the ear pinna be pulled downward and backward for a child under three years old?

options.A: The eardrum sits at a completely different angle in infants
options.B: It prevents the child from turning their head sideways
options.C: Children have more earwax blocking the upper canal
options.D: Their ear canal is shorter and straighter compared to an adult

explanation: An infant's ear canal anatomy requires a downward and backward pull to properly align the passage for drops. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h2)

question: Which type of mental ability actually tends to stay stable or even improve as people grow older?

options.A: Physical reaction speed during sudden emergency events
options.B: Crystallized intelligence based on accumulated life experience
options.C: Short-term working memory for complex math equations
options.D: Immediate recall of random, unrelated lists of numbers

explanation: Wisdom comes with age! Crystallized intelligence relies on stored knowledge and life experience, which stays strong or even grows as people get older.

question: Your patient knows how to inject their own insulin, but they need you to teach them how to calculate food portions. Which of Orem's systems is this?

options.A: Environmental control system
options.B: Supportive-educative system
options.C: Partially compensatory system
options.D: Fully compensatory system

explanation: Well done! In a supportive-educative system, the patient can do most things themselves, but they still need guidance, teaching, and support from you.

question: You are caring for an unconscious patient with a severe brain injury. Which nursing action best prevents aspiration?

options.A: Removing all oral secretions using a tongue blade
options.B: Laying the patient flat on their back to rest
options.C: Keeping the head of the bed elevated at 30 to 45 degrees
options.D: Feeding small pureed meals every two hours

explanation: Gravity is your friend here! Elevating the bed stops stomach contents and saliva from flowing back into the lungs.

question: What is the most common immediate complication right after an FGM procedure?

options.A: Osteoporosis in later adulthood
options.B: Severe bleeding and acute pain
options.C: Gestational diabetes mellitus
options.D: Chronic hypertension

explanation: Spot on! Cutting sensitive genital tissue with basic tools typically causes immediate, heavy bleeding and intense pain.

question: Which body fluid is usually NOT covered under standard precautions?

options.A: Vomitus
options.B: Saliva
options.C: Sweat
options.D: Urine

explanation: Great try! Sweat doesn't carry bloodborne infections, so unless there is visible blood in it, standard precautions don't apply to it.

question: On which side of the body should a patient hold a single-point walking cane?

options.A: Alternating hands with every step
options.B: Always in the dominant hand
options.C: The weak side of the body
options.D: The strong side of the body

explanation: Holding the cane on the strong side allows the patient to lean weight onto the device while moving the weaker leg forward. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h4)

question: Where is the substantia nigra physically located in the central nervous system?

options.A: At the base of the spinal cord
options.B: Within the midbrain
options.C: Inside the cerebral cortex
options.D: Directly inside the lateral ventricles

explanation: The substantia nigra is a dark-pigmented nucleus located in the midbrain that produces dopamine for the basal ganglia circuits. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T12#GNS211_U3_T12_h1)

question: Why should a nurse explain neurological tests using simple, non-medical terms?

options.A: To shorten the overall duration of the hospital stay
options.B: To reduce patient anxiety and improve cooperation
options.C: To replace the need for a physical examination
options.D: To avoid documenting the assessment in the medical record

explanation: Clear and simple communication helps calm the patient so they can participate fully and accurately in the assessment. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h2)

question: A teenage girl visits the clinic with recurrent chest infections and unusual linear burns across her breasts. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Breast ironing abuse
options.B: A severe allergic skin rash
options.C: Normal adolescent development
options.D: Accidental kitchen scalding

explanation: Unusual burn patterns and repeated infections on the chest during puberty are classic signs of breast ironing. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T17#GNS312_U1_T17_h6)

question: A menopausal patient has vaginal spotting and mild burning. What is the most likely cause of her cervical sensitivity?

options.A: Hyperactive cellular growth in the transformation zone
options.B: Frequent use of harsh chemical douches for hygiene
options.C: Lower estrogen levels causing thinning and drying of mucosal tissue
options.D: Increased production of thick mucus blocking the cervical canal

explanation: Well done! After menopause, lower estrogen makes the tissues thinner, drier, and much easier to irritate.

question: Which of the following is NOT a common barrier to effective clinical problem solving?

options.A: Fatigue and physical burnout
options.B: Heavy workloads and rushed decisions
options.C: Adequate staffing and clear communication
options.D: Fear of making mistakes and facing blame

explanation: Adequate staffing and clear communication help problem solving rather than acting as a barrier. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h5)

question: Why are drugs like carboprost or ergometrine only given AFTER the baby is born?

options.A: They lower maternal blood pressure to dangerous levels before the baby is born
options.B: They neutralize oxytocin and cause prolonged labour delay
options.C: They immediately stop all pain perception, making the mother unable to push
options.D: They cause violent, sustained uterine contractions that can rupture the uterus and harm the fetus

explanation: These powerful drugs clamp down the uterus hard to stop bleeding. If given before birth, they would cut off the baby's oxygen supply!

question: Why do nurses sometimes hesitate to ask patients about their spiritual needs?

options.A: Lack of available paperwork charts in the nursing station
options.B: Patients always refuse to answer questions about faith
options.C: Fear of imposing personal values or causing offense
options.D: Strict hospital policies forbidding any talk of religion

explanation: It's totally normal to worry about crossing boundaries, but being gentle and respectful makes spiritual care safe and meaningful for the patient.

question: What does 'informed consent' actually mean for a client undergoing a health screening?

options.A: They agree to take any medication prescribed after the test
options.B: They promise to pay all hospital bills within twenty-four hours
options.C: They sign a paper without reading it because the doctor told them to
options.D: They understand the risks, benefits, and purpose of the test before agreeing

explanation: You got it! Informed consent means the patient truly understands what is happening and freely agrees to it.

question: What is an effective way for a nurse to uncover a patient's hidden fears?

options.A: Assuming the patient is fine if they do not complain
options.B: Waiting until the doctor makes the primary diagnosis
options.C: Checking only the temperature chart every four hours
options.D: Asking open-ended questions about their current concerns

explanation: Spot on! Asking open questions like 'How are you feeling about everything?' gives patients a safe space to share worries they might otherwise hide.

question: How do vital signs usually change when a patient has severe fluid loss (hypovolemia)?

options.A: Heart rate increases and blood pressure drops
options.B: Both heart rate and blood pressure drop significantly
options.C: Both heart rate and blood pressure increase
options.D: Heart rate drops and blood pressure rises

explanation: Spot on! With less fluid in the pipes, blood pressure falls, and the heart races to try and keep circulation moving.

question: A patient with possible incomplete abortion has a fast heart rate (120 bpm) and low blood pressure (90/60 mmHg). What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Monitor for signs of hemorrhage and hypovolemic shock
options.B: Document the findings in the chart and wait until morning
options.C: Prepare the patient for a routine dietary consultation
options.D: Discharge the patient home with mild pain relievers

explanation: A fast pulse and low BP in a bleeding patient are major warning signs of heavy blood loss. Catching shock early saves lives!

question: What happens at the pyramidal decussation in the medulla oblongata?

options.A: Motor fibers cross over to the opposite side
options.B: Cranial nerve nuclei merge into a single structure
options.C: Oxygen exchange occurs for brain tissue
options.D: Cerebrospinal fluid is filtered out of the blood

explanation: Decussation is just a fancy word for crossing over! Here, most of the motor pathways cross to the opposite side of the body, which is why the left brain controls the right side of the body.

question: Which of these is NOT a normal use for sedative medications?

options.A: Treating bacterial infections
options.B: Stopping active epileptic seizures
options.C: Managing acute and chronic anxiety
options.D: Inducing sleep during short-term insomnia

explanation: Sedatives only calm the nervous system. They do not kill bacteria—that is a job for antibiotics! [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h4)

question: A village has no clinic, and residents must travel hours on bad roads just to get basic vaccines. What is the best way to solve this spatial barrier?

options.A: Outreach mobile health clinics visiting the community regularly
options.B: Closing all remaining health posts and telling patients to move to the city
options.C: Waiting for the community to build a multi-story teaching hospital
options.D: Punishing residents for failing to travel to town for healthcare

explanation: Brilliant! Mobile clinics bring care directly to the people, bypassing the challenge of bad roads and long distances.

question: Which nursing action compromises the accuracy of a fluid balance chart?

options.A: Waiting until the end of the shift to guess and write down intake amounts
options.B: Involving the patient and family in reporting oral drinks
options.C: Converting all cup and bowl volumes into milliliters promptly
options.D: Notifying the doctor immediately about a sudden drop in urine output

explanation: Relying on memory causes missed entries and incorrect data that jeopardize patient safety. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h8)

question: What is the best way for a community nurse to stop the spread of diarrhoea in a village?

options.A: Providing mosquito nets for sleeping areas at night
options.B: Teaching proper handwashing with soap and safe water storage
options.C: Inspecting local houses for structural roof damage
options.D: Distributing high-dose antibiotic capsules to all households

explanation: Diarrhoea germs usually spread through the faecal-oral route via dirty hands and water. Simple hygiene education and clean water storage save lives!

question: What is the primary digestive function of the oral cavity?

options.A: Absorption of complex carbohydrates into the bloodstream
options.B: Production of powerful hydrochloric acid to sterilize food
options.C: Complete enzymatic breakdown and absorption of proteins
options.D: Mechanical breakdown of food and mixing it with saliva

explanation: The mouth starts digestion by chewing food into smaller pieces and mixing it with saliva to create an easy-to-swallow bolus. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T1#GNS121_U1_T1_h1)

question: You are getting ready to shock with a manual defibrillator. What is the right sequence right before pressing the discharge button?

options.A: Charge the machine, announce 'clear', and visually check the team
options.B: Pause compressions, check the pulse, and apply gel pads
options.C: Administer emergency epinephrine and remove oxygen tubing
options.D: Turn off the mechanical ventilator and disconnect all IV lines

explanation: Safety first! Always charge the machine, shout a loud 'clear!', and double-check with your eyes that nobody is touching the patient before you hit that button.

question: Which of these is a very common challenge facing patient referrals in Nigeria?

options.A: An overabundance of working ambulances in every village
options.B: Excessive availability of free medication at tertiary hospitals
options.C: Too many doctors available at primary healthcare centers
options.D: High transportation costs and poor road infrastructure

explanation: You know this context well! Bad roads and expensive transport fares often cause heartbreaking delays for patients trying to reach referral centers.

question: A depressed patient says that life feels completely hopeless. What is the best, most therapeutic way to reply?

options.A: It sounds like you are carrying a very heavy burden right now. Let us talk about it.
options.B: Do not worry about it, many people feel much worse than you do.
options.C: Everything will look much brighter tomorrow once you get some sleep.
options.D: You have so many things to be grateful for, so try not to feel down.

explanation: Wonderful! Validating their feelings without dismissing them builds trust and opens the door for a truly helpful conversation.

question: What is the very FIRST thing a nurse should do when a patient suddenly gets severe shortness of breath?

options.A: Help the patient sit up and check their oxygen delivery
options.B: Leave the room immediately to find the attending doctor
options.C: Document the exact time the symptoms started
options.D: Have the patient lie flat on their back for rest

explanation: Patient comfort and breathing come first! Always help them sit upright and check their oxygen before you start writing notes or running off.

question: Which physical sign strongly points to pelvic inflammation around the Pouch of Douglas?

options.A: Cervical motion tenderness
options.B: Positive Murphy sign
options.C: Upper right quadrant tenderness
options.D: Absent bowel sounds

explanation: You're doing great. When the pelvic tissues and the Pouch of Douglas are inflamed, gently moving the cervix jostles them and causes sharp pain.

question: What is the main sign that someone has a drug abuse problem?

options.A: Using vitamins for daily nutritional balance
options.B: Consuming natural herbs for mild headaches
options.C: Harmful or hazardous use despite negative consequences
options.D: Taking prescribed medications strictly as directed

explanation: Drug abuse means a person keeps using a substance even when it clearly harms their health, relationships, or daily life. You've got this!

question: What is the main goal of primary prevention in neurological nursing?

options.A: To rehabilitate a patient after a massive stroke
options.B: To cure advanced stages of Alzheimer's disease
options.C: To stop a neurological disease before it starts
options.D: To detect brain tumors through early screening tests

explanation: Think of primary prevention as your shield. It focuses entirely on health promotion and stopping conditions from developing in the first place.

question: Which maternal blood vessels are opened up by the placenta to bathe the fetal villi in nutrient-rich blood?

options.A: Cardinal veins
options.B: Uterine veins
options.C: Umbilical arteries
options.D: Spiral arteries

explanation: Spot on! The trophoblast gently remodels the mother's spiral arteries so that blood pools nicely around the baby's villi for easy sharing.

question: Why is it important to screen food handlers for typhoid?

options.A: It prevents food handlers from catching the disease from customers
options.B: Chronic carriers can shed the bacteria in their stool without showing symptoms
options.C: It stops the bacteria from mutating into a virus
options.D: Food handlers are legally required to take daily antibiotics

explanation: Spot on! Some people carry the bacteria without feeling sick, so screening food handlers stops them from unknowingly spreading it to others.

question: What is a major risk of spending too much time under strong ultraviolet (UV) sunlight?

options.A: Faster regeneration of damaged subcutaneous tissue
options.B: Enhanced production of protective surface lipids
options.C: Increased risk of skin cancers and premature aging
options.D: Permanent increase in the skin's moisture content

explanation: Correct! UV rays mess with skin cell DNA, which over time can cause early wrinkles and serious skin growths.

question: What is the main focus of manipulative and body-based therapies like massage?

options.A: The ingestion of raw botanical extracts
options.B: The manipulation of external spiritual energy fields
options.C: The physical structures and systems of the body
options.D: The psychological regulation of deep breathing

explanation: Well done! These therapies focus directly on working with the physical body parts, such as muscles and bones through massage or chiropractic care.

question: Why must clinicians be very cautious when giving Class IC drugs to a patient with a history of a heart attack?

options.A: These drugs will immediately cause the patient's blood pressure to drop to zero
options.B: The damaged heart muscle will completely neutralize the drug within five minutes
options.C: Strong sodium blockade can provoke dangerous new arrhythmias in damaged heart tissue
options.D: Class IC medications only work when mixed with high doses of intravenous potassium

explanation: Class IC drugs slow conduction so drastically that they can cause fatal rhythm problems in structurally damaged hearts. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h3)

question: Why is routine urinalysis important during pregnancy checkups?

options.A: It checks for protein and sugar, which show kidney stress or diabetes
options.B: It measures the heartbeat of the unborn baby
options.C: It tells the nurse the exact weight of the placenta
options.D: It proves whether the mother is eating enough vegetables

explanation: Protein in urine can point to pre-eclampsia, while sugar can point to diabetes, both needing close management. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T8#GNS225_U3_T8_h5)

question: Which problem is most likely to happen if someone has a severe lack of dietary fat?

options.A: Dangerous spikes in blood sugar
options.B: Trouble absorbing vitamins A, D, E, and K
options.C: An enlarged thyroid gland
options.D: Too much good cholesterol in the blood

explanation: Remember, fat-soluble vitamins need dietary fat to get absorbed! Without enough fat, deficiency symptoms start to show up.

question: A patient is prescribed an inhaled bronchodilator and an inhaled corticosteroid. In what order should they take them?

options.A: Corticosteroid in the morning and bronchodilator only at bedtime
options.B: Both medications mixed together in the nebulizer at the same time
options.C: Corticosteroid first, wait a few minutes, then the bronchodilator
options.D: Bronchodilator first, wait a few minutes, then the corticosteroid

explanation: Open the door first! Taking the bronchodilator opens up the airways so the steroid that follows can travel much deeper into the lungs to fight inflammation.

question: Why are national implementation committees necessary for primary health care?

options.A: To prescribe individual drugs to rural patients
options.B: To set standard policies, coordinate donor support, and evaluate nationwide health goals
options.C: To replace local government chairmen during elections
options.D: To manage the daily cleaning of every village health post

explanation: National committees ensure uniformity in health service delivery, manage national funds, and guide the overall direction of the country's health sector. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T7#GNS124_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which lobe of the cerebral cortex is primarily responsible for processing visual information?

options.A: Occipital lobe
options.B: Parietal lobe
options.C: Temporal lobe
options.D: Frontal lobe

explanation: The back of the brain, known as the occipital lobe, specializes in receiving and making sense of what the eyes see. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h3)

question: Why shouldn't you give an expectorant to someone with a dry, non-productive cough?

options.A: Dry coughs do not involve trapped mucus that needs loosening
options.B: Dry coughs always require strong narcotic suppression instead
options.C: It will permanently damage the delicate lining of the trachea
options.D: The medication will cause severe allergic reactions in the throat

explanation: You got it! Since there's no mucus present in a dry cough, an expectorant has nothing to work on and won't help the patient.

question: How often should an IV insertion site covered with a transparent dressing be visually inspected by the nurse?

options.A: Whenever the patient complains of severe pain
options.B: Only once every seven days
options.C: Only when changing the IV solution bag
options.D: During every routine shift assessment

explanation: Frequent visual checks through transparent dressings allow nurses to catch early signs of redness, swelling, or infiltration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h8)

question: What is a common sign that prompts a patient to suspect they might have a tapeworm?

options.A: Passing flat, white worm segments in the stool
options.B: Coughing up blood-stained sputum during the night
options.C: Noticing painful swelling in the lower limbs
options.D: Developing severe jaundice in the eyes and skin

explanation: Spot on! Patients often notice moving or detached worm segments (proglottids) in their toilet visits, which is usually what brings them to the clinic.

question: What is the main laboratory test used to detect chlamydia and gonorrhea from a swab or urine sample?

options.A: Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests
options.B: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
options.C: Stool occult blood analysis
options.D: Complete blood count with differential

explanation: NAATs are the gold standard! They accurately copy and spot tiny amounts of the germ's genetic material.

question: Which safe imaging tool is essential during antenatal visits to check where the placenta is attached?

options.A: Amniocentesis
options.B: Fetal scalp electrode
options.C: Pelvic X-ray
options.D: Ultrasonography

explanation: An ultrasound is a safe, non-painful way to look inside, check the exact spot where the placenta sits, and make sure it isn't growing too deep.

question: What is a major duty of a healthcare social worker?

options.A: Connecting patients with financial aid and community resources
options.B: Administering daily intravenous antibiotics
options.C: Designing physical exercise routines for stroke recovery
options.D: Performing physical examinations and diagnosing illnesses

explanation: Social workers step in to solve non-medical worries, such as finding financial support, housing, or community help for older patients.

question: What do we call the main nutrients that give the body bulk energy and building blocks?

options.A: Antioxidants
options.B: Electrolytes
options.C: Micronutrients
options.D: Macronutrients

explanation: Great job! Macronutrients include carbs, proteins, and fats. They are the big players that supply your daily energy and physical structure.

question: Which finding strongly suggests a testicular rupture after a heavy blow to the scrotum?

options.A: Painless enlargement of both testicles over a period of several weeks
options.B: Clear watery drainage leaking from a small scratch on the scrotal skin
options.C: Loss of the normal outline of the testicle on ultrasound with severe local tenderness
options.D: Complete inability to control bowel movements after the impact

explanation: When the testicle bursts, it loses its smooth oval shape on an ultrasound scan, and the patient will have intense pain and swelling. You're mastering trauma assessments!

question: What does severe, lasting swelling in a pregnant woman's lower legs usually tell you?

options.A: Normal muscle growth in the lower extremities
options.B: Potential fluid retention and vascular complications
options.C: A sign of high physical activity and exercise
options.D: Excessive intake of clean drinking water

explanation: A little swelling can happen towards the end of pregnancy, but heavy or persistent swelling (edema) is a red flag to check her blood pressure for pre-eclampsia.

question: Why is seeing a patient at home more revealing than seeing them in a hospital clinic?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any health teaching
options.B: It gives the nurse access to advanced laboratory equipment
options.C: It shows their true daily living conditions and family dynamics
options.D: It forces the patient to follow medical advice strictly

explanation: The home environment exposes real-life challenges like food storage, safety hazards, and family support systems that clinics hide. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T11#GNS225_U2_T11_h1)

question: Which conflict resolution style results in a win-win solution where both parties' needs are fully met?

options.A: Smoothing
options.B: Competing
options.C: Collaboration
options.D: Avoiding

explanation: Collaboration involves open communication and problem-solving to satisfy all concerns, creating a true win-win outcome. [learn more](GST321_U1_T13#GST321_U1_T13_h7)

question: Why is establishing a patient baseline important during a cardiovascular assessment?

options.A: It removes the need to perform future physical examinations
options.B: It helps the nurse notice sudden changes in the patient's condition
options.C: It proves that the doctor's diagnosis is always completely correct
options.D: It lowers the overall cost of hospital admission for the client

explanation: Knowing a patient's normal state allows the nurse to quickly spot abnormal shifts that signal worsening heart trouble. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the standard core rights of medication administration?

options.A: Right dose
options.B: Right manufacturer
options.C: Right time
options.D: Right patient

explanation: The core medication rights focus on the patient, drug, dose, route, time, and documentation, rather than the specific company that manufactured the product. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of youth-friendly health services?

options.A: To replace pediatric care units in large hospitals
options.B: To attract, reach, and retain young people in care
options.C: To provide free surgical procedures for teenagers
options.D: To enforce mandatory health screenings for school children

explanation: Youth-friendly services are specifically designed to overcome the barriers that usually keep teenagers away from traditional health facilities. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T18#GNS312_U3_T18_h1)

question: What is the best way for a nurse to accurately track fluid balance for a pregnant patient with acute kidney injury?

options.A: Using an indwelling urinary catheter for strict hourly output measurement
options.B: Asking the patient to estimate how many times she urinates each day
options.C: Weighing the patient once every morning after breakfast
options.D: Checking skin turgor and mucous membrane moisture every shift

explanation: When kidneys are in trouble, hourly checks via catheter give us the exact numbers we need to see if treatments are working.

question: How do modern communities (like online student groups) change our view of physical borders?

options.A: Individuals can no longer feel attached to their neighborhoods
options.B: Physical maps are no longer used by any government agencies
options.C: Geographical borders completely disappear during public health emergencies
options.D: People can form connected groups based on shared interests without living near each other

explanation: Today, technology and social media let people connect and support each other across long distances, stretching beyond just physical location.

question: A community health nurse notices a sudden rush of parents requesting routine check-ups for young girls right before long school holidays. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Families preparing daughters for upcoming FGM ceremonies
options.B: Standard preventive screening recommended by public health
options.C: A sudden regional outbreak of adolescent infections
options.D: Parents seeking routine sports physicals for school teams

explanation: School holidays are prime time when families travel home or arrange for girls to undergo FGM. Always stay alert for these patterns in community practice!

question: Which type of transmission happens when tiny germ particles float in the air over long distances?

options.A: Vector-borne transmission
options.B: Airborne transmission
options.C: Direct contact
options.D: Droplet transmission

explanation: You've got it! Airborne germs are super tiny and can ride the air currents across a room.

question: Why is it helpful for nurses to understand the emotional shifts pregnant women go through?

options.A: To replace the need for routine physical examinations
options.B: To diagnose underlying psychiatric personality disorders
options.C: To distinguish normal milestones from clinical distress
options.D: To prevent hormonal fluctuations from occurring entirely

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Knowing what's typical helps you reassure moms and catch true mental health needs early on.

question: What classic set of signs points to cardiac tamponade?

options.A: Slow pulse, flushed skin, and high temperature
options.B: High BP, strong pulses, and clear breath sounds
options.C: Fast breathing, pinpoint pupils, and quiet tummy
options.D: Low BP, muffled heart sounds, and swollen neck veins

explanation: Known as Beck's triad, these three signs (low blood pressure, muffled heart tones from fluid, and distended neck veins) are huge red flags for tamponade! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h7)

question: What happens to the amount of virus (viral load) during the long, quiet chronic latency stage of HIV?

options.A: It drops to lower levels compared to the acute stage
options.B: It increases rapidly every single day
options.C: It remains exactly identical to the acute stage peak
options.D: It disappears completely from the bloodstream

explanation: Great job! During latency, the viral load settles down compared to the massive spike during early infection, though the virus is still quietly active.

question: How can you, as a nurse, best figure out if a home care client is feeling socially isolated?

options.A: Measuring the client's blood pressure and heart rate
options.B: Asking who the client interacts with or talks to during the week
options.C: Reviewing the client's past surgical history in the hospital chart
options.D: Checking the expiration dates on the client's kitchen food

explanation: Sometimes the best assessment tool is simply asking! Direct and friendly questions help you see just how much human contact they actually get.

question: What do we call the process where we stop noticing a constant, unchanging smell after a while?

options.A: Sensory transduction
options.B: Olfactory hallucination
options.C: Receptor depolarization
options.D: Olfactory adaptation

explanation: You nailed it! Olfactory adaptation is why you stop noticing your own perfume or room freshener after being around it for a few minutes.

question: Why are deep animal bites often left open instead of being stitched tightly right away?

options.A: To prevent trapping bacteria inside a closed space and causing an abscess
options.B: Because sutures dissolve too quickly when exposed to animal saliva
options.C: To allow the patient to apply their own herbal ointments at home
options.D: Because closed wounds take longer to form a dry scab

explanation: If you seal a dirty bite closed, you trap bacteria inside a warm, cozy pocket where they can easily form a nasty abscess.

question: Why is a literature review considered weak if it only lists article summaries one by one?

options.A: It fails to show how the studies connect, contradict, or answer the main research question
options.B: It takes too much time to format correctly in standard APA style
options.C: It violates international copyright laws regarding academic journals
options.D: It forces the reader to look up all the original articles themselves

explanation: A simple list lacks deep analysis. True synthesis connects different findings to show broader patterns in the science.

question: Why must a triage nurse keep monitoring patients who are waiting in the emergency queue?

options.A: Doctors refuse to see patients without updated charts
options.B: Waiting patients often complain about the slow service
options.C: A stable patient's condition can suddenly get worse
options.D: Hospital policy requires a vital sign check every five minutes

explanation: Illness can change quickly! Someone who looks stable at first triage can crash suddenly and need immediate help. Keep a close eye on your patients.

question: What do we call the swelling that happens when fluid gets trapped in body tissues?

options.A: Atrophy
options.B: Sclerosis
options.C: Oedema
options.D: Necrosis

explanation: Spot on! Oedema is just the clinical word for when excess fluid builds up in the spaces between your body tissues, causing that puffy look.

question: What is the best feeding advice for a breastfed baby who gets diarrhoea?

options.A: Continue breastfeeding on demand without interruption
options.B: Wait twenty-four hours before offering breast milk again
options.C: Dilute breast milk with equal parts sterile water
options.D: Stop breastfeeding and switch to plain water only

explanation: Keep feeding! Breast milk gives the baby both hydration and essential nutrients to fight off the infection and stay strong.

question: A patient is admitted with suspected lymphoma. What is the most common early physical sign a nurse expects to find?

options.A: Severe skin rashes over the tummy
options.B: Painless, enlarged lymph nodes in the neck
options.C: Complete paralysis of both legs
options.D: Bleeding gums and sudden nosebleeds

explanation: Keep an eye out for this: the earliest and most common sign is a lump in the neck that swells up without causing any pain.

question: What is the term for the natural home where a germ lives, grows, and multiplies?

options.A: Susceptible host
options.B: Reservoir
options.C: Vector
options.D: Portal of exit

explanation: Spot on! A reservoir is like a cozy home or breeding ground where germs hang out, survive, and multiply before finding a new victim.

question: How can nurses safely manage IV fluids when electronic infusion pumps aren't available?

options.A: By using gravity drip sets paired with frequent manual monitoring of flow rates
options.B: By clamping the intravenous line completely shut for hours at a time
options.C: By squeezing the intravenous fluid bag continuously by hand until empty
options.D: By substituting all intravenous therapy with oral water ingestion

explanation: Gravity infusion sets plus regular, careful checks help nurses control flow safely even without fancy hospital equipment.

question: What is a dangerous emergency complication for patients with high spinal cord injuries, often triggered by something simple like a full bladder?

options.A: Autonomic dysreflexia
options.B: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.C: Malignant hyperthermia
options.D: Acute respiratory alkalosis

explanation: That's right! Autonomic dysreflexia causes a sudden, life-threatening spike in blood pressure triggered by discomfort below the injury, such as a full bladder or tight clothing.

question: Why don't we use syrup of ipecac anymore to treat poisoning?

options.A: It is too expensive to manufacture
options.B: It causes unpredictable vomiting and risks aspiration
options.C: It permanently stains the lining of the stomach
options.D: It neutralizes all known hospital antidotes

explanation: Ipecac causes vomiting at random, delayed times. If the patient vomits and breathes it into their lungs (aspiration), it can cause serious damage, so it's a no-go today.

question: Why do endocrine problems usually cause a full-body crisis instead of just a local issue?

options.A: Hormones only work when the patient is under severe stress
options.B: Endocrine organs are all connected directly to the brain
options.C: Hormones travel through the bloodstream to affect many organs
options.D: Endocrine glands store large amounts of toxic waste products

explanation: Think of hormones like mail carriers circulating through the blood vessels. Because they travel everywhere, trouble in just one gland can quickly shake up multiple body systems at once!

question: What position should a patient be in when receiving oral medications?

options.A: Upright sitting position
options.B: Flat on their back
options.C: Lying on their left side
options.D: Bent over at the waist

explanation: An upright or elevated sitting position uses gravity to help the patient swallow safely and prevents choking. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h6)

question: What happens when you empower nurses in a clinical unit?

options.A: Reduced need for continuing education programs
options.B: Increased professional autonomy and job satisfaction
options.C: Complete elimination of shift handovers
options.D: Shorter educational requirements for new graduates

explanation: Empowerment gives nurses the confidence to make sound clinical decisions, which makes them happier and more fulfilled in their jobs!

question: What is the main difference between monitoring and evaluation in public health projects?

options.A: Monitoring costs a lot of money, while evaluation is completely free
options.B: Monitoring is done only by doctors, while evaluation is done by patients
options.C: Monitoring is continuous tracking, while evaluation measures final outcomes against objectives
options.D: Monitoring focuses on finance, while evaluation focuses entirely on building roads

explanation: Monitoring happens all through the project to keep things on track, whereas evaluation looks back to see if goals were met. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h9)

question: How often should you reposition a bedbound patient to keep pressure ulcers away?

options.A: Every six hours
options.B: Every two hours
options.C: Once per shift
options.D: Every 30 minutes

explanation: You got it! Turning your patient at least every two hours takes the heavy pressure off bony areas and gets the blood flowing to their skin again.

question: What is the immediate danger when a person's upper airway gets blocked?

options.A: High blood pressure all over the body
options.B: Too much lung fluid being made
options.C: Blocked airflow leading to low oxygen (hypoxia)
options.D: The tiny air sacs in the lower lungs get too big

explanation: When the upper airway is blocked, fresh air can't get through to the lungs. This causes oxygen levels in the blood to drop fast—a condition we call hypoxia.

question: Which part of the brain is the main control center for the vomiting reflex?

options.A: Cerebellum
options.B: Cerebral cortex
options.C: Hypothalamus
options.D: Medulla oblongata

explanation: Great job! The vomiting center sits right in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem, pulling together different nerve signals to trigger vomiting. You've got this!

question: A patient is on strict bed rest. What is the most effective nursing action to prevent bedsores (pressure injuries)?

options.A: Applying thick layers of adhesive bandages over the heels
options.B: Massaging reddened bony prominences vigorously with alcohol
options.C: Repositioning the patient on a regular two-hour schedule
options.D: Turning the patient only once during the night shift

explanation: Turning patients every two hours takes the pressure off bony areas, keeping the skin healthy and intact. Brilliant nursing care!

question: You walk into a warm ward and notice a patient is shivering and moving very slowly. Which condition should pop into your head?

options.A: Diabetes mellitus
options.B: Cushing syndrome
options.C: Hyperthyroidism
options.D: Hypothyroidism

explanation: When the thyroid is underactive, internal heat production drops. That's why these patients often feel freezing cold and sluggish, even when everyone else is comfortable.

question: What early signs do women with ovarian cancer most often report to their doctors?

options.A: High fever, chills, and purulent vaginal discharge
options.B: Sudden, sharp, localized stabbing pain in the right lower quadrant
options.C: Painful urination and visible blood in the urine
options.D: Vague digestive changes, bloating, and early fullness when eating

explanation: Good job! These symptoms can easily feel like a normal tummy upset, which is why early detection is tricky.

question: Why is secondary adrenal insufficiency caused by pituitary problems so dangerous for a patient?

options.A: Blood sugar shoots up dangerously high because of a lack of balance.
options.B: The kidneys suddenly stop filtering waste products out of the blood.
options.C: Lacking ACTH makes the adrenal glands stop producing vital cortisol.
options.D: The heart rate goes completely out of control without nerve signals.

explanation: Without ACTH telling them what to do, the adrenal glands shrink and stop making cortisol. That leaves the body completely unable to handle stress, which can quickly lead to shock.

question: What is the main benefit of regular team meetings among different healthcare professionals in an SNF?

options.A: To coordinate diverse professional insights and prevent conflicting care plans
options.B: To reduce the number of visitors allowed in the facility
options.C: To allow administrators to review employee attendance records
options.D: To replace the need for daily nursing assessments and vital sign checks

explanation: When nursing, therapy, and kitchen staff meet together, everyone works toward the exact same patient goals. Teamwork makes the dream work!

question: What defines an orphan drug?

options.A: A medication developed to treat a rare medical condition
options.B: An herbal supplement with no scientific research backing
options.C: A controlled substance classified under Schedule I rules
options.D: A drug that has been abandoned by the manufacturing company

explanation: Orphan drugs are specifically created to help patients suffering from rare diseases that affect few people. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T1#GNS125_U2_T1_h7)

question: Where do the nerve fibers in the dorsal column pathway cross over to the opposite side of the body?

options.A: The lumbar spinal cord
options.B: The peripheral skin receptor
options.C: The medulla oblongata
options.D: The cerebral cortex

explanation: Spot on! As these sensory messages travel up, they cross over to the other side once they reach the lower part of the brainstem called the medulla.

question: What is the proper way to clean the delicate lens on an infrared thermometer?

options.A: Submerge the whole device in boiling water for five minutes
options.B: Spray high-pressure air directly onto the glass
options.C: Scrub the lens firmly with a scouring pad
options.D: Wipe gently with an approved alcohol wipe following maker instructions

explanation: A gentle wipe with isopropyl alcohol cleans the lens safely without scratching the glass or frying the electronics.

question: How many months in a row without a period must pass before menopause is officially confirmed?

options.A: 24 months
options.B: 18 months
options.C: 6 months
options.D: 12 months

explanation: Doctors and nurses look backward: once a woman goes a full 12 consecutive months without bleeding, menopause is officially confirmed.

question: Which type of shock is directly caused by a massive loss of circulating blood volume?

options.A: Anaphylactic shock
options.B: Cardiogenic shock
options.C: Hypovolemic shock
options.D: Obstructive shock

explanation: Think of the prefix 'hypo' (low) and 'volume' (fluid). Hypovolemic shock happens when there just isn't enough fluid or blood left in the pipes, usually due to heavy bleeding or severe dehydration.

question: Which of these is part of the external male reproductive system?

options.A: Seminal vesicle
options.B: Prostate gland
options.C: Vas deferens
options.D: Scrotum

explanation: The scrotum and the penis are on the outside (external), while the prostate, vas deferens, and seminal vesicles are tucked inside the body.

question: Which factor is part of an environmental safety assessment for a client with balance problems?

options.A: Checking for loose rugs, poor lighting, and stairs
options.B: Checking the color of the paint on the bedroom walls
options.C: Counting the number of chairs in the living room
options.D: Measuring the room temperature and humidity levels

explanation: Environmental checks focus on removing physical hazards like tripping risks to prevent falls at home. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T5#GNS222_U3_T5_h7)

question: Why is it smart to call the receiving hospital on the phone before sending an emergency patient?

options.A: To confirm the exact home address of the ambulance driver
options.B: To ask the doctor on duty for permission to use their hospital ambulance
options.C: To ensure the receiving team can prepare equipment and space for the patient
options.D: To negotiate the medical bills before the patient arrives at the gate

explanation: A quick heads-up phone call lets the hospital prep a bed, oxygen, or blood products before the ambulance even rolls through their gates.

question: How does carbon dioxide travel away from the fetus?

options.A: It travels through the maternal lymphatic system only
options.B: It diffuses across the placental membrane into maternal blood
options.C: It is stored safely inside the amniotic fluid until birth
options.D: It is actively pumped out by the umbilical arteries

explanation: CO2 is a small molecule that easily slips (diffuses) right across the membrane from the baby's tiny blood vessels into the mother's blood to be breathed out by her lungs. [learn more](GNS121_U6_T5#GNS121_U6_T5_h4)

question: Why would a doctor order a diagnostic thoracentesis?

options.A: To measure how much oxygen the lungs can hold total
options.B: To find out the exact cause of a pleural fluid buildup
options.C: To prevent the development of a future heart attack
options.D: To permanently cure chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

explanation: Great thinking! When we take a little sample of that fluid to the lab, we can figure out why it started gathering in the chest in the first place.

question: Which family planning method helps protect against both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections?

options.A: Subdermal implants
options.B: Copper intrauterine devices
options.C: Latex condoms
options.D: Progestin-only pills

explanation: Condoms act as a physical barrier that blocks both sperm and infectious agents. Simple and effective!

question: Why is accurate handover documentation legally important for you as a nurse?

options.A: It prevents the nursing council from inspecting the hospital
options.B: It serves as evidence that patient care and responsibilities were properly transferred
options.C: It guarantees that the nurse will never be questioned by a doctor
options.D: It allows the hospital to charge higher fees for room maintenance

explanation: Clear notes protect you legally by proving you handed over patient duties responsibly and professionally.

question: On a histogram, what does the vertical axis (Y-axis) usually stand for?

options.A: The individual patient identification numbers
options.B: The specific names of nursing units
options.C: The frequency or count of observations
options.D: The calendar dates of data collection

explanation: Think of the Y-axis as the counter: it tells you how many times a certain value or range popped up.

question: How can a nurse help a client who is struggling with transportation to a clinic appointment?

options.A: Connecting her with affordable clinic options or community support
options.B: Telling her that missing the appointment has no health consequences
options.C: Insisting that she buy a personal vehicle before discharge
options.D: Advising her to walk several miles alone in the hot afternoon sun

explanation: Practical problems like transport can stop mums from getting care. Helping them find nearby or affordable options makes a huge difference.

question: At what point should a sharps disposal container be closed and replaced to keep everyone safe?

options.A: One-quarter full
options.B: Halfway full
options.C: Completely filled to the brim
options.D: Three-quarters full

explanation: Never overfill a sharps bin! Closing it when it's three-quarters full ensures protruding needles won't accidentally prick anyone.

question: Why is stomach cancer often found at a late stage?

options.A: Diagnostic imaging tests cannot visualize the inner stomach lining.
options.B: Tumors in the stomach grow much faster than in any other organ.
options.C: Early symptoms closely mimic common, benign stomach issues like gastritis.
options.D: Patients routinely refuse endoscopy procedures until they bleed.

explanation: Exactly! Because early signs look just like normal heartburn or mild gastritis, people often brush it off until the tumor grows larger.

question: Why is data screening necessary before conducting statistical analysis?

options.A: To catch entry errors and missing values that could distort results
options.B: To make the dataset large enough for international publication
options.C: To eliminate the need for any ethical approval board review
options.D: To change patient outcomes so the research hypothesis is proven right

explanation: Screening ensures that impossible entries or typos do not ruin the accuracy of the final research findings. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h6)

question: How do automated hospital beds make a nurse's duty easier?

options.A: By eliminating the need to ever document vital signs manually
options.B: By completely replacing the need for bedside nursing assistants
options.C: By making regular patient safety rounds completely unnecessary
options.D: By reducing physical strain during patient repositioning and transfers

explanation: Patient beds with automated features do the heavy lifting when turning or moving patients, saving your back from unnecessary strain!

question: Which of these is NOT a typical drying side effect of anticholinergic drugs like meclizine or scopolamine?

options.A: Excessive salivation
options.B: Dry mouth
options.C: Urinary retention
options.D: Blurred vision

explanation: That's right! Anticholinergones dry things up, so you get dry mouth, not excessive drooling. Think 'can't spit, can't pee, can't see, can't stool' for anticholinergics!

question: Why do nurse researchers find ogive graphs useful when looking at health data?

options.A: They calculate exact individual medication dosages
options.B: They show totals that build up above or below certain values
options.C: They replace the need for writing patient clinical notes
options.D: They prove a direct cause-and-effect relationship in a trial

explanation: Spot on! Ogives let us easily track how numbers pile up (accumulate) across a set of clinical measurements.

question: Which bone is located at the very back of a baby's skull?

options.A: The occipital bone
options.B: The frontal bone
options.C: The sphenoid bone
options.D: The temporal bone

explanation: Spot on! The occipital bone sits at the back and forms the lower base and rear part of the skull.

question: Which organs take the biggest hit from long-term iron overload caused by frequent blood transfusions?

options.A: Lungs, pleura, and upper airways
options.B: Brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves
options.C: Liver, heart, and endocrine glands
options.D: Stomach, intestines, and pancreas

explanation: Extra iron loves to settle down in hard-working organs like the liver, the heart muscle, and hormone-making glands, eventually causing tissue damage if not treated.

question: Which part of the brain connects the nervous system to the endocrine system?

options.A: Cerebral cortex
options.B: Medulla oblongata
options.C: Hypothalamus
options.D: Cerebellum

explanation: The hypothalamus is the master bridge! It takes messages from the brain and turns them into hormonal orders.

question: Why is proper injection safety so important for nurses?

options.A: Injections are rare procedures that need special certification
options.B: Injections are done daily and can spread serious infections if mishandled
options.C: Hospital management uses injection logs to grade nursing speed
options.D: Patients expect disposable equipment for financial reasons

explanation: You'll give lots of injections! Because they happen so often, even a tiny slip in safety can quickly pass an infection to many people. Staying sharp keeps everyone safe.

question: What is the main feature that separates chronic osteomyelitis from acute osteomyelitis?

options.A: The complete inability of bacteria to cause tissue damage
options.B: The duration of the infection lasting for months or years
options.C: The restriction of the disease to flat facial bones
options.D: The total absence of any pain or localized swelling

explanation: The big difference is time! Chronic means it has been hanging around stubbornly for months or even years.

question: What is the main job of our respiratory system?

options.A: Producing red blood cells
options.B: Bringing in oxygen and removing carbon dioxide
options.C: Regulating body temperature
options.D: Filtering bacteria out of the bloodstream

explanation: Spot on! The lungs trade gases with every breath we take—bringing in fresh oxygen our body loves and blowing out waste carbon dioxide.

question: How does long-term high blood pressure in the lungs (pulmonary hypertension) directly change the heart?

options.A: It shrinks the left atrium because less blood returns from the lungs
options.B: It causes the heart valves to stretch and leak due to low blood pressure
options.C: It weakens the left ventricle by reducing blood flow through the aorta
options.D: It causes the right ventricle to thicken and enlarge from working too hard

explanation: You've got it! Just like lifting heavy weights makes a bicep grow, the right ventricle bulks up (hypertrophies) when it has to push against high lung pressures. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h6)

question: A healthy newborn is crying vigorously in the delivery room. Which circulatory change is happening to help oxygenate the blood?

options.A: Pulmonary blood vessels constrict to push blood back
options.B: Fetal shunts close to direct blood through the lungs
options.C: Systemic blood pressure drops to zero
options.D: The liver stops receiving blood supply temporarily

explanation: When the baby takes its first breath, lung vessels open up and fetal shunts close so that blood goes directly to the lungs for oxygen. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h2)

question: A newborn has a heart rate of 110, pink body with blue hands, a strong cry, and pulls away when touched. What score do they get for muscle tone (Activity)?

options.A: Score of 1 for some flexion
options.B: Score of 2 for weak cry
options.C: Score of 0 for limp tone
options.D: Score of 2 for active motion

explanation: Active movement and good flexion of the arms and legs show great muscle tone, earning the full 2 points in the Apgar activity check. You've got this!

question: Which of these is a good example of objective documentation during a reproductive assessment?

options.A: Patient seems overly anxious and does not like pelvic exams
options.B: Skin intact, no lesions or abnormal discharge noted on the labia
options.C: Patient is probably hiding symptoms due to personal embarrassment
options.D: External genitalia look completely normal and healthy overall

explanation: Spot on! Objective notes focus on clear, observable facts rather than personal guesses or vague opinions.

question: What is the main goal of planning emergency transport and money before labor starts?

options.A: To replace the need for professional skilled attendants at birth
options.B: To guarantee that the mother will have a completely painless delivery
options.C: To eliminate costly delays when unexpected complications strike
options.D: To ensure the baby is born precisely on the expected due date

explanation: Exactly right! Having transport and funds ready ahead of time saves precious minutes and prevents dangerous delays if an emergency happens.

question: A patient arrives at the emergency ward in severe pain and struggling to breathe. What should the nurse do about medication education right now?

options.A: Postpone detailed teaching until the patient is stable and comfortable
options.B: Force the patient to read a long pamphlet immediately
options.C: Give the medication silently without any explanation ever
options.D: Ask family members to sign a waiver ignoring the teaching

explanation: Severe pain and distress make it impossible to focus or remember things. Always stabilize the patient first before trying to teach!

question: Which nursing action helps calm a patient's fear of the unknown before a procedure?

options.A: Telling the patient not to ask any questions
options.B: Giving clear, simple explanations about what will happen
options.C: Leaving the room immediately after administering medication
options.D: Keeping all details secret until the exact moment of the test

explanation: Brilliant! Demystifying the procedure by explaining things simply takes away the scary mystery and lowers anxiety.

question: What is the maximum recommended time limit for a single intubation attempt to protect the patient?

options.A: 30 seconds
options.B: 5 minutes
options.C: 2 minutes
options.D: 10 minutes

explanation: Limiting attempts to 30 seconds prevents prolonged interruption of oxygen delivery and avoids severe hypoxia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h4)

question: A patient says, 'I cannot be healthy because I am too weak to go to work and look after my children.' Which health model are they using?

options.A: Clinical model
options.B: Role performance model
options.C: Eudaimonistic model
options.D: Biological germ model

explanation: Spot on! This model measures health by whether a person can successfully carry out their daily family and job responsibilities.

question: What is the main goal of using the 'teach-back' method with a patient?

options.A: To replace the need for written discharge leaflets
options.B: To fulfill mandatory hospital documentation quotas
options.C: To test the patient's ability to read medical textbooks
options.D: To verify that the patient truly understood the instructions

explanation: Asking them to explain your instructions back in their own words helps you catch any misunderstandings before they go home.

question: Which of these is a key community role for a nurse promoting safe motherhood?

options.A: Manufacturing routine pharmaceutical drugs
options.B: Managing hospital financial budgets
options.C: Performing major obstetric surgeries alone
options.D: Health education and mobilizing families

explanation: You got it! Teaching families about danger signs and encouraging them to visit the clinic early is one of our best community tools.

question: In many homes, unfair food sharing puts which group at the highest risk of poor nutrition?

options.A: Young children and pregnant or lactating women.
options.B: Older teenage boys who play sports.
options.C: Elderly grandparents who live independently.
options.D: Adult male wage earners who work outside the home.

explanation: You're right! Even though their bodies need extra nutrients for growth and health, these groups often end up with the smallest shares.

question: Why can stopping a long-term sedative suddenly trigger seizures?

options.A: The sudden lack of medication causes permanent damage to the heart muscle
options.B: The liver immediately releases stored toxins directly into the bloodstream
options.C: Blood pressure drops to zero because the blood vessels lose all tone
options.D: Removing the drug causes a rebound of extreme nervous system overactivity

explanation: When you take away the medication that was keeping the brain calm, the nervous system bounces back with a wild surge of activity. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h6)

question: A patient with an enlarged prostate is most likely to experience which problem?

options.A: Complete inability to produce testosterone
options.B: Permanent loss of the sense of thirst
options.C: Severe pain during the production of new sperm
options.D: Difficulty starting and maintaining a urine stream

explanation: Because the prostate surrounds the urethra, swelling or enlargement pinches the tube and obstructs urine flow. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T3#GNS121_U4_T3_h3)

question: You check an IV site and notice it is swollen, cool to the touch, and painful while the pump is running. What's happening?

options.A: An air bubble has triggered the internal line sensor
options.B: The medication is working at its optimal therapeutic level
options.C: The pump battery is failing and needs to be replaced
options.D: Fluid has leaked into the surrounding tissue (infiltration)

explanation: Spot on! Cool, swollen, and painful tissue around the site means the fluid is going into the arm tissue instead of the vein. Time to stop the infusion and restart!

question: A nurse wants to teach a rural community how to prevent cholera. What is the best way to communicate?

options.A: Distribute dense medical textbooks written in advanced technical English.
options.B: Post warning notices exclusively on international websites.
options.C: Use local languages and collaborate with respected community leaders.
options.D: Rely entirely on unspoken signs posted without any translation.

explanation: People listen best to trusted community voices speaking in their own language. Communication is key in public health!

question: Why might you suggest a patient eating plant-based iron (like beans or greens) drink a glass of orange juice with their meal?

options.A: Orange juice contains phytates that bind extra minerals
options.B: Citrus acid coats the stomach lining to prevent cramping
options.C: The sugar in the juice speeds up overall stomach emptying
options.D: Vitamin C in the juice enhances the absorption of plant-based iron

explanation: Brilliant! Vitamin C gives plant iron a chemical makeover that makes it way easier for your gut to absorb.

question: What does the letter 'B' stand for in the SBAR communication tool?

options.A: Bedside
options.B: Behavior
options.C: Background
options.D: Briefing

explanation: Spot on! 'B' stands for Background, giving the history and context that led up to the current issue.

question: When is the best time to perform airway suctioning on a ventilated patient?

options.A: When clinical indicators like secretions or coughing are present
options.B: Every single hour on the exact hour without fail
options.C: Only when the high-pressure alarm rings twice
options.D: Immediately before every meal or tube-feeding cycle

explanation: We don't suction on a rigid schedule because it can irritate the airway and lower oxygen levels. Instead, we listen, assess, and suction only when the patient actually needs it.

question: What happens when antibodies in a patient's plasma encounter unfamiliar red blood cell antigens?

options.A: They convert the foreign antigens into safe body proteins
options.B: They absorb the extra antigens to nourish surrounding tissues
options.C: They dissolve the donor red blood cells into liquid plasma
options.D: They bind to the foreign cells and cause agglutination

explanation: Plasma antibodies attack unfamiliar antigens by latching onto them, which makes the red blood cells clump together. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h1)

question: Why is stepping on the scale to check daily body weight so crucial in the care plan for kidney failure?

options.A: It measures how well the bone marrow is producing red blood cells.
options.B: It helps calculate the exact amount of protein the patient needs to eat.
options.C: It is the most sensitive daily indicator of fluid retention or loss.
options.D: It indicates whether the patient is taking their iron supplements on time.

explanation: Numbers don't lie! A sudden weight gain over a day or two almost always means the kidneys are struggling and the body is holding onto dangerous amounts of fluid.

question: You are getting a ventilated, unstable patient ready for a CT scan. What is your most important safety check?

options.A: Turning off all continuous intravenous drug infusions to save battery life
options.B: Ensuring portable oxygen, monitor, and emergency equipment are fully functional
options.C: Removing all patient identification bands to prevent scanning delays
options.D: Notifying the hospital cafeteria that the patient will miss lunch

explanation: Always make sure your transport life support gear is fully charged and working so you are ready for anything while away from the ICU.

question: What is an essential nursing intervention during the postoperative recovery phase for a patient undergoing surgical repair of a vesicovaginal fistula?

options.A: Applying dry heat packs directly to the perineal suture line
options.B: Encouraging heavy ambulation immediately after surgery
options.C: Maintaining continuous bladder drainage to keep the surgical site dry
options.D: Removing urinary catheters as soon as the patient wakes up

explanation: Keeping the bladder empty via a catheter prevents urine pressure from disrupting the delicate new suture line while it heals. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T16#GNS312_U1_T16_h6)

question: During body development before birth, the labia majora grow from the exact same tissue that forms which male structure?

options.A: The vas deferens
options.B: The seminal vesicles
options.C: The scrotum
options.D: The prostate gland

explanation: Fascinating, right? Embryology shows us how different structures develop from the same root tissues. The labia majora correspond to the male scrotum!

question: Why are frequent neurovascular checks so important for a patient in cervical traction?

options.A: To check if the patient is sleeping enough hours
options.B: To detect early signs of spinal cord or nerve compression
options.C: To prevent the skin from turning yellow
options.D: To measure how much water the patient is drinking

explanation: You want to catch any nerve trouble early! Checking movement and feeling in the arms and hands keeps the patient safe from permanent injury.

question: What is a crucial safety rule to remember when giving a therapeutic or medicated bath?

options.A: Leaving the patient completely unattended so they can relax
options.B: Making the water as hot as possible to open up the pores fully
options.C: Avoiding the use of any towels after the patient steps out
options.D: Limiting the bath duration to prevent skin maceration and exhaustion

explanation: Remember, soaking too long can waterlog fragile skin and totally wear out a patient who is already weak from illness. Keep an eye on the clock!

question: Why do tablets or injections (systemic drugs) often struggle to treat eye problems effectively?

options.A: Blood vessels in the eye destroy active ingredients
options.B: Unique barriers like the cornea block them from getting inside
options.C: Systemic drugs cannot dissolve in body fluids
options.D: The liver breaks down all eye medications too quickly

explanation: Think of the eye as a well-guarded fort! Natural barriers like the cornea make it hard for drugs travelling through your bloodstream to get inside the eye in strong enough amounts.

question: What makes malaria an example of biological vector-borne transmission?

options.A: The mosquito only carries the parasite on the outside of its physical legs
options.B: The malaria parasite develops and multiplies inside the mosquito before being injected
options.C: The malaria pathogen is spread purely through human-to-human coughing
options.D: The disease can only live inside warm-blooded animal reservoirs

explanation: In biological transmission, the parasite undergoes a necessary part of its life cycle inside the vector before it can infect a new host. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h6)

question: You visit a diabetic patient and notice their insulin is stored next to open food in a messy kitchen. What should you do?

options.A: Report the family to the local police department for negligence
options.B: Immediately discharge the patient from the home care program
options.C: Educate the patient and family on safe medication storage and hygiene
options.D: Leave the medication where it is since it is their private home

explanation: As a nurse, you are a teacher! Patient and family education fixes safety risks gently while respecting their living situation. Well done.

question: What is the main difference between a direct and an indirect obstetric death?

options.A: Direct deaths occur during labor, while indirect deaths occur in the postpartum period
options.B: Direct deaths are caused by infections, while indirect deaths are caused by bleeding
options.C: Direct deaths happen in the hospital, while indirect deaths happen at home
options.D: Direct deaths are from pregnancy complications, while indirect deaths are from pre-existing diseases worsened by pregnancy

explanation: Spot on! Direct causes come straight from pregnancy or childbirth issues (like bleeding), while indirect causes happen when a pre-existing condition (like heart disease or malaria) gets worse because of the pregnancy.

question: What is the top nursing priority right after major cancer surgery?

options.A: Withdrawing all intravenous fluids immediately
options.B: Preventing complications and managing acute surgical pain
options.C: Discharging the patient within twenty-four hours
options.D: Starting intensive physical exercise right away

explanation: Right after surgery, keeping your patient comfortable and watching out for issues like infection or blood clots are your most important duties. You are well on your way to becoming an amazing nurse!

question: In Nigerian public health, what does the acronym IDSR stand for?

options.A: Infectious Disease Sanitation Routine
options.B: Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response
options.C: Immediate District Symptom Record
options.D: International Drug Safety Regulation

explanation: Correct! IDSR is the helpful framework our health facilities use to track, report, and respond to important diseases efficiently.

question: Why should a nurse avoid crushing an enteric-coated tablet?

options.A: It turns the solid pill into an unmixable powder
options.B: It changes the color of the liquid mixture
options.C: It causes the medication to dissolve too slowly
options.D: It ruins the special coating designed to protect the stomach

explanation: Enteric coatings protect the stomach lining from irritation or protect the drug from stomach acid; crushing destroys this barrier. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why is teaching a practical skill alone often not enough for economic empowerment?

options.A: Most skills taught in centers are already outdated within one month.
options.B: Government laws forbid disabled individuals from owning private businesses.
options.C: Skills training causes physical fatigue that worsens disability.
options.D: Trainees also need startup capital, equipment, and market access to succeed.

explanation: Learning a trade is brilliant, but without the right tools and a way to sell their goods or services, graduates will still struggle to generate income.

question: What is informed consent truly about in clinical research?

options.A: An ongoing conversation between the researcher and the participant
options.B: A form filed away where patients never see it
options.C: A guarantee that the study will cure the patient
options.D: A one-time legal paper signed at the hospital door

explanation: You got it! Informed consent isn't just a paper signature; it is a continuous, friendly dialogue from start to finish.

question: Which of the following is an example of a three-dimensional instructional aid?

options.A: An audio podcast
options.B: A chalkboard drawing
options.C: A printed textbook page
options.D: Anatomical manikin

explanation: Three-dimensional aids have length, breadth, and thickness, allowing students to touch and examine physical structures like manikins and models. [learn more](GST321_U8_T4#GST321_U8_T4_h3)

question: Which of the deep cerebellar nuclei is the largest and helps us plan complex movements?

options.A: Emboliform nucleus
options.B: Globose nucleus
options.C: Fastigial nucleus
options.D: Dentate nucleus

explanation: The dentate nucleus is the biggest of the bunch! It takes info from the outer cerebellar hemispheres to help coordinate smooth, planned movements. You're doing brilliantly.

question: What is the main job of a structured healthcare network in reproductive health?

options.A: Eliminating the need for patient medical records across facilities
options.B: Replacing all traditional birth attendants with certified surgeons
options.C: Generating revenue for private pharmaceutical manufacturing companies
options.D: Linking different levels of care to ensure seamless service delivery

explanation: Spot on! Healthcare networks connect primary clinics to big hospitals so patients glide smoothly through the system for whatever care they need.

question: What is the very first thing you must do when the AED tells everyone to 'stand clear'?

options.A: Check the patient's pulse at the carotid artery.
options.B: Press the shock button immediately without waiting.
options.C: Administer a rescue breath using a bag-valve-mask.
options.D: Ensure nobody is touching the patient.

explanation: Safety first! If anyone is touching the patient, the AED might misread the heart rhythm—or worse, give someone else a shock.
